1. Genetic Algorithm Workflow for Solving the 8-Queens Problem

The 8-Queens problem is a classic combinatorial optimization benchmark that requires placing eight chess queens on an \(8 \times 8\) chessboard such that no two queens attack each other vertically, horizontally, or diagonally. Genetic Algorithms (GAs) solve this search problem by mimicking biological evolution, using stochastic search operators over a population of candidate solutions.

The execution workflow progresses iteratively through generation cycles until a zero-conflict configuration is discovered or the maximum generation count is reached. The high-level architecture of the GA workflow is depicted below:

graph TD A[Initial Population Generation] --> B[Evaluate Fitness of Population] B --> C{Termination Criteria Met?} C -- Yes --> D[Output Best Solution] C -- No --> E[Selection: Roulette / Tournament] E --> F[Crossover / Recombination] F --> G[Mutation Operator] G --> H[Form New Population Generation] H --> B

2. Detailed Genetic Algorithm Mechanics

a) Chromosome Representation

To eliminate vertical attacks by construction, each individual chromosome is represented as an array of 8 integers \(C = [r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4, r_5, r_6, r_7, r_8]\), where index \(i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 8\}\) represents the column position and the value \(r_i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 8\}\) specifies the row position of the queen in column \(i\). This guarantees exactly one queen per column.

b) Fitness Function

The total number of unique pairs of queens on an 8-queen board is given by \(\binom{8}{2} = 28\). The fitness function \(f(C)\) measures the number of non-attacking queen pairs. A solution is found when \(f(C) = 28\).

Mathematical formulation of attacks:

  • Horizontal Attack: Queens at column \(i\) and \(j\) attack horizontally if \(r_i = r_j\).
  • Diagonal Attack: Queens at column \(i\) and \(j\) attack diagonally if \(|r_i - r_j| = |i - j|\).

Thus, the fitness function is formulated as:

\[ f(C) = 28 - \sum_{1 \le i < j \le 8} \text{Attack}(i, j) \]

where \(\text{Attack}(i, j) = 1\) if \(r_i = r_j\) or \(|r_i - r_j| = |i - j|\), and \(0\) otherwise.

c) Selection

Roulette Wheel Selection assigns a probability of selection \(P(C_k)\) to chromosome \(C_k\) proportional to its relative fitness within a population of size \(N\):

\[ P(C_k) = \frac{f(C_k)}{\sum_{m=1}^{N} f(C_m)} \]

d) Crossover (Recombination)

With crossover probability \(p_c \approx 0.8\), two parent chromosomes are sliced at a random crossover point \(k \in \{1, \dots, 7\}\). For instance, with single-point crossover at point 3:

  • Parent 1: [2, 4, 6 | 8, 1, 3, 5, 7]
  • Parent 2: [1, 3, 5 | 2, 7, 4, 8, 6]
  • Offspring 1: [2, 4, 6 | 2, 7, 4, 8, 6]
  • Offspring 2: [1, 3, 5 | 8, 1, 3, 5, 7]

e) Mutation

To avoid local minima, each gene in an offspring undergoes mutation with a low probability \(p_m \approx 0.05\). Mutation alters a queen's row assignment \(r_i\) to a random new value in \(\{1, \dots, 8\}\).

1. Natural Language Processing (NLP) Parsing Techniques

Parsing in Natural Language Processing involves determining the syntactic structure of a text according to a formal grammar. Parsing algorithms transform linear strings of words into structured syntactic trees (parse trees). Two fundamental paradigms exist: Top-Down Parsing and Bottom-Up Parsing, with dynamic programming extensions like Chart Parsing (e.g., Earley and CYK parsers) addressing efficiency constraints.

Top-Down Parsing vs. Bottom-Up Parsing

  • Top-Down Parsing: Starts from the start symbol \(S\) of the context-free grammar (CFG) and applies production rules downwards to match terminal words in the sentence. It is goal-driven but suffers from backtracking issues and potential infinite loops with left-recursive grammar rules.
  • Bottom-Up Parsing: Starts directly from the terminal tokens of the input sentence and applies grammar rules in reverse (reductions) up to the root symbol \(S\). It is data-driven but can explore syntactically valid local trees that cannot form a valid overall sentence.
  • Chart Parsing (Dynamic Programming): Both top-down and bottom-up methods re-parse duplicate sub-phrases. Chart parsers employ an Edge Chart (well-formed substring table) to store completed constituent parses, achieving \(O(n^3)\) worst-case time complexity.
graph TD S["S (Sentence)"] --> NP1["NP (Noun Phrase)"] S --> VP["VP (Verb Phrase)"] NP1 --> Det1["Det (Determiner)"] NP1 --> N1["N (Noun)"] Det1 --> W1["The"] N1 --> W2["robot"] VP --> V["V (Verb)"] VP --> NP2["NP (Noun Phrase)"] V --> W3["moved"] NP2 --> Det2["Det (Determiner)"] NP2 --> N2["N (Noun)"] Det2 --> W4["the"] N2 --> W5["box"]

2. Context-Free Grammar Parsing for 'The robot moved the box'

Consider the Context-Free Grammar \(G = (V, \Sigma, R, S)\) defined by:

  • Non-terminals (\(V\)): \(\{S, NP, VP, Det, N, V\}\)
  • Terminals (\(\Sigma\)): \(\{\text{"The"}, \text{"robot"}, \text{"moved"}, \text{"the"}, \text{"box"}\}\)
  • Start Symbol: \(S\)
  • Production Rules (\(R\)):
    \(S \rightarrow NP \ VP\)
    \(NP \rightarrow Det \ N\)
    \(VP \rightarrow V \ NP\)
    \(Det \rightarrow \text{"The" \mid "the"}\)
    \(N \rightarrow \text{"robot" \mid "box"}\)
    \(V \rightarrow \text{"moved"}\)

Step-by-Step Parse Derivation (Top-Down Execution):

  1. Expand root \(S \rightarrow NP \ VP\).
  2. Expand left-most symbol \(NP \rightarrow Det \ N\).
  3. Match terminals: \(Det \rightarrow \text{"The"}\) matches token 1 ("The").
  4. Match terminals: \(N \rightarrow \text{"robot"}\) matches token 2 ("robot"). Concludes first \(NP\).
  5. Expand remaining symbol \(VP \rightarrow V \ NP\).
  6. Match terminal: \(V \rightarrow \text{"moved"}\) matches token 3 ("moved").
  7. Expand second \(NP \rightarrow Det \ N\).
  8. Match terminals: \(Det \rightarrow \text{"the"}\) matches token 4 ("the") and \(N \rightarrow \text{"box"}\) matches token 5 ("box").

The derivation succeeds completely, producing the full hierarchical syntax tree shown above.

1. Expert System Development for Medical Diagnosis (MYCIN / PROSPECTOR)

Expert Systems are knowledge-based AI applications designed to emulate human expert decision-making in specific domains such as medical diagnosis (MYCIN) and geological exploration (PROSPECTOR). The architecture decouples domain-specific knowledge from reasoning mechanisms, allowing incremental updates.

graph LR User[User / Clinician] <--> UI[User Interface] UI <--> IE[Inference Engine] IE <--> KB[(Knowledge Base: Rules & Facts)] IE <--> WM[Working Memory / Patient Data] IE <--> EF[Explanation Facility]

Key structural components include:

  • Knowledge Base: Contains heuristic domain knowledge encoded as production rules (IF-THEN clauses).
  • Inference Engine: Executes goal-driven forward chaining (data-driven) or backward chaining (hypothesis-driven diagnosis).
  • Working Memory: Contains patient-specific symptoms, test results, and dynamically derived conclusions.
  • Explanation Facility: Provides transparency by answering "WHY" a question is asked or "HOW" a diagnosis was reached.

2. Certainty Factors (CF) and Rule Chaining

Medical diagnosis operates under uncertainty due to incomplete or noisy diagnostic tests. MYCIN introduced the Certainty Factor (CF) model, defining CF as the difference between the Measure of Belief (\(MB\)) and Measure of Disbelief (\(MD\)):

\[ CF(H, E) = MB(H, E) - MD(H, E) \]

where \(CF \in [-1, +1]\). A value of \(+1\) indicates absolute certainty of hypothesis \(H\), \(-1\) indicates absolute falsehood, and \(0\) represents total ignorance.

Mathematical Rules for CF Combination and Propagation:

  1. Conjunction of Evidences (AND): \[ CF(E_1 \land E_2) = \min(CF(E_1), CF(E_2)) \]
  2. Disjunction of Evidences (OR): \[ CF(E_1 \lor E_2) = \max(CF(E_1), CF(E_2)) \]
  3. Rule Propagation (Single Rule): For rule \(R: \text{IF } E \text{ THEN } H \text{ (with weight } CF_{rule}\text{)}\): \[ CF(H, E) = CF(E) \times CF_{rule} \quad (\text{if } CF(E) > 0) \]
  4. Combining Multiple Independent Rules for Hypothesis \(H\): Given \(CF_1\) and \(CF_2\) supporting \(H\): \[ CF_{comb}(CF_1, CF_2) = \begin{cases} CF_1 + CF_2(1 - CF_1) & \text{if } CF_1, CF_2 > 0 \\ \frac{CF_1 + CF_2}{1 - \min(|CF_1|, |CF_2|)} & \text{if one is positive, one negative} \\ CF_1 + CF_2(1 + CF_1) & \text{if } CF_1, CF_2 < 0 \end{cases} \]

1. STRIPS Planning Algorithm in the Block World Domain

The Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver (STRIPS) is a automated planning framework that represents world states as conjunctions of first-order literals and actions using precondition-effect schemas. STRIPS uses goal-stack planning—a recursive stack-based search technique that solves subgoals sequentially using means-ends analysis.

STRIPS Action Operator Components:

  • Preconditions: Predicates that must hold true in the current state for the action to be executed.
  • Add List: Predicates that become true after executing the action.
  • Delete List: Predicates that cease to be true after executing the action.
graph TD A[Pop top element from Goal Stack] --> B{Is top element a State Predicate?} B -- Yes & True in Current State --> C[Pop Predicate] B -- Yes & False in Current State --> D[Push satisfying Action & its Preconditions to Stack] B -- No (It is an Action) --> E[Execute Action: Update State with Add/Delete Lists] E --> F[Record Action in Plan]

2. Step-by-Step Plan Generation Trace

Consider a Block World instance with blocks \(A\) and \(B\):

  • Initial State \(S_0\): \(\{OnTable(A), OnTable(B), Clear(A), Clear(B), HandEmpty\}\)
  • Goal State \(G\): \(\{On(A, B)\}\)

STRIPS Operators:

  • Pickup(\(x\)): Precond: \(\{Clear(x), OnTable(x), HandEmpty\}\); Add: \(\{Holding(x)\}\); Del: \(\{OnTable(x), Clear(x), HandEmpty\}\).
  • Stack(\(x, y\)): Precond: \(\{Holding(x), Clear(y)\}\); Add: \(\{On(x, y), HandEmpty, Clear(x)\}\); Del: \(\{Holding(x), Clear(y)\}\).

Execution Stack Trace:

  1. Push goal \(On(A, B)\) to Goal Stack.
  2. To achieve \(On(A, B)\), select operator \(\text{Stack}(A, B)\). Push \(\text{Stack}(A, B)\) and its preconditions \(\{Holding(A), Clear(B)\}\) to stack.
  3. Check top subgoal \(Clear(B)\): True in \(S_0\). Pop \(Clear(B)\).
  4. Check subgoal \(Holding(A)\): False in \(S_0\). Select operator \(\text{Pickup}(A)\). Push \(\text{Pickup}(A)\) and its preconditions \(\{Clear(A), OnTable(A), HandEmpty\}\).
  5. Check preconditions \(\{Clear(A), OnTable(A), HandEmpty\}\): All True in \(S_0\). Pop preconditions.
  6. Execute \(\text{Pickup}(A)\): Update state: \(S_1 = \{Clear(B), Holding(A)\}\). Add \(\text{Pickup}(A)\) to Plan.
  7. Execute \(\text{Stack}(A, B)\): Update state: \(S_2 = \{On(A, B), Clear(A), HandEmpty\}\). Add \(\text{Stack}(A, B)\) to Plan.

Final Plan Generated: \([\text{Pickup}(A), \text{Stack}(A, B)]\).

1. Reinforcement Learning: Q-Learning Algorithm

Q-Learning is a model-free, off-policy temporal difference (TD) reinforcement learning algorithm designed to learn the optimal action-value function \(Q^*(s, a)\) for a Markov Decision Process (MDP). It does not require a prior model of environmental transition dynamics.

The agent learns by interacting with the environment, maintaining a Q-table containing estimated cumulative future rewards for taking action \(a\) in state \(s\). The Q-value update rule is derived from the Bellman Optimality Equation:

\[ Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha \left[ r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a) \right] \]

where \(\alpha \in (0, 1]\) is the learning rate, \(\gamma \in [0, 1)\) is the discount factor, \(r\) is the immediate reward, and \(s'\) is the next state reached.

2. 3-Step Q-Table Trace for Grid-World Pathfinding

Consider a \(2 \times 2\) Grid-World with states \(S_1(1,1)\), \(S_2(1,2)\), \(S_3(2,1)\), and Goal state \(S_4(2,2)\). Let parameters be \(\alpha = 0.5\), \(\gamma = 0.9\), and initial Q-table values \(Q(s, a) = 0\) for all \((s, a)\).

Reward structure: Step cost \(r = -1\), reaching goal state \(S_4\) gives reward \(r = +10\).

graph LR S1["S1 (1,1)"] -- Right --> S2["S2 (1,2)"] S1 -- Down --> S3["S2 (2,1)"] S2 -- Down --> S4["S4 (Goal)"] S3 -- Right --> S4["S4 (Goal)"]

Trace Execution:

  • Step 1: Agent in \(S_1\), takes action Right, moves to \(S_2\). Reward \(r = -1\). \[ Q(S_1, \text{Right}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.5 \left[ -1 + 0.9 \max_{a'} Q(S_2, a') - 0 \right] = 0.5[-1 + 0] = -0.5 \]
  • Step 2: Agent in \(S_2\), takes action Down, reaches Goal \(S_4\). Reward \(r = +10\). \[ Q(S_2, \text{Down}) \leftarrow 0 + 0.5 \left[ 10 + 0.9(0) - 0 \right] = 0.5[10] = 5.0 \]
  • Step 3: Agent resets to \(S_1\), takes action Right again, moves to \(S_2\). Reward \(r = -1\). \[ Q(S_1, \text{Right}) \leftarrow -0.5 + 0.5 \left[ -1 + 0.9 \max_{a'} Q(S_2, a') - (-0.5) \right] \]

    Since \(\max_{a'} Q(S_2, a') = Q(S_2, \text{Down}) = 5.0\):

    \[ Q(S_1, \text{Right}) \leftarrow -0.5 + 0.5 \left[ -1 + 0.9(5.0) + 0.5 \right] = -0.5 + 0.5 [ -1 + 4.5 + 0.5 ] = -0.5 + 2.0 = 1.5 \]

Updated Q-table values: \(Q(S_1, \text{Right}) = 1.5\), \(Q(S_2, \text{Down}) = 5.0\).

1. Dempster-Shafer Theory for Sensor Fusion

Dempster-Shafer (D-S) Theory of Evidence is a mathematical framework for reasoning with uncertainty that generalizes Bayesian probability by allowing beliefs to be assigned to sets of hypotheses (subsets of a universal frame of discernment \(\Theta\)) rather than singletons alone. It handles ignorance and conflicting sensor data effectively in multi-sensor fusion applications.

Core Definitions:

  • Frame of Discernment (\(\Theta\)): A finite set of mutually exclusive hypotheses. The power set \(2^\Theta\) represents all possible propositions.
  • Basic Probability Assignment (BPA / Mass Function \(m\)): A mapping \(m: 2^\Theta \rightarrow [0, 1]\) satisfying: \[ m(\emptyset) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{A \subseteq \Theta} m(A) = 1 \]
  • Belief Function (\(Bel(A)\)): The total belief committed to hypothesis \(A\) and its subsets: \[ Bel(A) = \sum_{B \subseteq A} m(B) \]
  • Plausibility Function (\(Pl(A)\)): The maximum extent to which belief could be committed to \(A\): \[ Pl(A) = \sum_{B \cap A \neq \emptyset} m(B) = 1 - Bel(\bar{A}) \]

2. Dempster's Rule of Combination & Calculations

Given independent mass assignments \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) from two sensors, Dempster's rule combines them into unified mass \(m_{1,2}(A)\):

\[ m_{1,2}(A) = \frac{\sum_{B \cap C = A} m_1(B) m_2(C)}{1 - K} \]

where conflict measure \(K = \sum_{B \cap C = \emptyset} m_1(B) m_2(C)\).

Hypothesis Set Calculation Example:

Let \(\Theta = \{A, B, C\}\). Sensor 1 yields \(m_1(\{A\}) = 0.6\), \(m_1(\Theta) = 0.4\). Sensor 2 yields \(m_2(\{A, B\}) = 0.7\), \(m_2(\Theta) = 0.3\).

m1 \ m2m2({A,B}) = 0.7m2(Θ) = 0.3
m1({A}) = 0.6{A} ∩ {A,B} = {A} (0.42){A} ∩ Θ = {A} (0.18)
m1(Θ) = 0.4Θ ∩ {A,B} = {A,B} (0.28)Θ ∩ Θ = Θ (0.12)

Conflict \(K = 0\). Combined masses:

  • \(m_{1,2}(\{A\}) = 0.42 + 0.18 = 0.60\)
  • \(m_{1,2}(\{A, B\}) = 0.28\)
  • \(m_{1,2}(\Theta) = 0.12\)

Calculating measures for subset \(\{A\}\):

  • \(Bel(\{A\}) = m_{1,2}(\{A\}) = 0.60\)
  • \(Pl(\{A\}) = m_{1,2}(\{A\}) + m_{1,2}(\{A, B\}) + m_{1,2}(\Theta) = 0.60 + 0.28 + 0.12 = 1.00\)

1. Knowledge Representation: Conceptual Graphs and Scripts

Structured knowledge representation frameworks capture complex relational and procedural knowledge. Conceptual Graphs (Sowa) and Scripts (Schank) provide expressive formalisms for natural language understanding and story comprehension.

Conceptual Graphs (CG) vs. Scripts

  • Conceptual Graphs: Directed bipartite networks consisting of Concept Nodes (representing entities, attributes, or states) and Conceptual Relation Nodes (linking concepts). Operations include Copy, Restrict, Join, and Simplify.
  • Scripts: Structured knowledge frames that encode stereotyped sequences of events in specific contexts, utilizing Conceptual Dependency (CD) primitives like PTRANS (physical transfer), INGEST (consuming), and ATRANS (transfer of ownership).

2. Script Representation for 'Restaurant Dining Experience'

A complete script details roles, props, preconditions, and chronological scenes:

graph TD A[Scene 1: Entering] --> B[Scene 2: Ordering] B --> C[Scene 3: Eating] C --> D[Scene 4: Paying & Exiting]

Script Structure: RESTAURANT

  • Track: Fast Casual / Standard Dining
  • Props: Tables, Menu, Food, Bill, Money
  • Roles: Customer (\(C\)), Waiter (\(W\)), Chef (\(F\)), Cashier (\(K\))
  • Entry Conditions: \(C\) is hungry; \(C\) has money.
  • Results: \(C\) is full; \(C\) has less money; Restaurant owner has more money.

Chronological Event Scenes:

  • Scene 1: Entering
    \(C\) PTRANS self into restaurant; \(C\) MOVE eyes to empty table; \(C\) PTRANS self to table; \(C\) SIT down on chair.
  • Scene 2: Ordering
    \(W\) ATRANS menu to \(C\); \(C\) MTRANS menu content to memory; \(C\) MTRANS decision to \(W\); \(W\) PTRANS order to Chef \(F\).
  • Scene 3: Eating
    \(F\) PREPARE food; \(W\) PTRANS food to \(C\); \(C\) INGEST food.
  • Scene 4: Paying & Exiting
    \(W\) ATRANS bill to \(C\); \(C\) ATRANS money/tip to \(W\); \(C\) PTRANS self out of restaurant.

1. Wumpus World Knowledge-Based Agent

The Wumpus World is a partially observable environment represented as a \(4 \times 4\) grid where an agent seeks gold while avoiding pits and the Wumpus. A Knowledge-Based (KB) Agent uses Propositional Logic to infer safe unvisited cells based on perceptual inputs.

Domain Logic Rules:

  • \(P_{i,j}\): Pit at cell \((i, j)\); \(B_{i,j}\): Breeze at cell \((i, j)\).
  • \(W_{i,j}\): Wumpus at cell \((i, j)\); \(S_{i,j}\): Stench at cell \((i, j)\).
  • Breeze Rule: A cell has a breeze if and only if an adjacent cell contains a pit: \[ B_{1,1} \iff (P_{1,2} \lor P_{2,1}) \]
  • Stench Rule: A cell has a stench if and only if an adjacent cell contains the Wumpus: \[ S_{1,1} \iff (W_{1,2} \lor W_{2,1}) \]

2. Trace of Logical Inference for Safe Cell Discovery

graph LR Cell11["[1,1] Perception: None"] --> Safe12["Infer [1,2] Safe"] Cell11 --> Safe21["Infer [2,1] Safe"] Safe21 --> Move21["Move to [2,1] Perception: Stench"] Move21 --> InferWumpus["Infer Wumpus at [3,1] or [2,2]"]

Inference Steps:

  1. At Cell [1,1]: Percept is \([\text{None}, \text{None}, \text{None}, \text{None}, \text{None}]\).
    • Agent knows \(\neg B_{1,1}\) and \(\neg S_{1,1}\).
    • From \(\neg B_{1,1} \iff \neg(P_{1,2} \lor P_{2,1})\), using De Morgan's Law: \(\neg P_{1,2} \land \neg P_{2,1}\).
    • Similarly, \(\neg W_{1,2} \land \neg W_{2,1}\).
    • Conclusion: Both \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) are completely safe.
  2. Move to Cell [2,1]: Percept is \([\text{Stench}, \text{None}, \text{None}, \text{None}, \text{None}]\).
    • Agent perceives \(S_{2,1}\), so \(S_{2,1} \implies (W_{1,1} \lor W_{3,1} \lor W_{2,2})\).
    • Since \(\neg W_{1,1}\) was established previously, KB derives \((W_{3,1} \lor W_{2,2})\).
    • Because \(\neg B_{2,1}\), we derive \(\neg P_{3,1}\) and \(\neg P_{2,2}\).
    • Conclusion: Cell \((2,2)\) has no pit, making it safe from pits for further exploration.

1. Machine Learning Paradigms

Machine Learning algorithms build models from empirical data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed. The four primary paradigms differ based on learning signals and supervisor feedback:

  • Supervised Learning: Learning from labeled paired datasets \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}\) to approximate mapping function \(f: X \rightarrow Y\). Examples: Classification, Regression.
  • Unsupervised Learning: Finding hidden intrinsic patterns, groupings, or representations from unlabeled data \(\{x_i\}\). Examples: Clustering (K-Means), Dimensionality Reduction (PCA).
  • Semi-Supervised Learning: Combines a small set of labeled data with a large volume of unlabeled data to improve accuracy while reducing labeling costs.
  • Reinforcement Learning: Goal-oriented learning where an agent takes actions in an environment to maximize cumulative reward using trial-and-error state transitions.

2. Comparative Analysis: K-Means Clustering vs. Support Vector Machines (SVM)

Feature K-Means Clustering Support Vector Machine (SVM)
Paradigm Unsupervised Learning Supervised Learning
Primary Objective Partition data into \(K\) cohesive clusters minimizing intra-cluster variance. Find optimal hyper-plane maximizing margin between classes.
Mathematical Formulation \[ \arg\min_{S} \sum_{i=1}^{K} \sum_{x \in S_i} \|x - \mu_i\|^2 \] \[ \min_{w, b} \frac{1}{2}\|w\|^2 \text{ s.t. } y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1 \]
Decision Boundaries Voronoi tessellation (spherical boundaries around cluster centroids). Linear or non-linear hyperplanes created via Kernel trick (RBF, Polynomial).
Outlier Sensitivity High; mean centroids easily distorted by noisy outliers. Low; decision boundary dependent primarily on support vectors.

1. System Architecture for an Autonomous Search & Rescue Drone

An intelligent autonomous drone operating in disaster zone search-and-rescue operations requires integrated hardware-software architecture for real-time perception, localization, path planning, and task execution under partial observability.

graph TD Sensors[Sensors: LiDAR, Thermal Camera, IMU, GPS] --> Fusion[Sensor Fusion: Extended Kalman Filter] Fusion --> StateEst[State & Map Estimation] StateEst --> PathPlanner[3D A* Path Planner] StateEst --> DecisionMaker[Bayesian Decision Model] PathPlanner --> Control[Flight Controller / Actuators] DecisionMaker --> Mission[Mission Goal Execution]

2. Technical Module Specifications

a) PEAS Framework Specification

  • Performance Measure: Number of survivors detected, time to complete mission, battery efficiency, collision avoidance rate.
  • Environment: Unstructured, GPS-denied indoor/outdoor disaster terrain, severe smoke, changing wind.
  • Actuators: Quadrotor brushless motors, pan-tilt camera gimbals, rescue beacon drop mechanism.
  • Sensors: 3D LiDAR, Thermal IR camera, RGB Camera, Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU), Ultrasonic Altimeter.

b) Sensor Fusion & Path Planning (A*)

Multi-sensor data is fused using an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for robust state estimation. Path planning in 3D grid space uses 3D A* search with Euclidean heuristic function:

\[ h(n) = \sqrt{(x_n - x_g)^2 + (y_n - y_g)^2 + (z_n - z_g)^2} \]

The evaluation function \(f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\) ensures optimal collision-free trajectory selection.

c) Knowledge Representation & Uncertainty Management

Survivor probability maps are maintained using a Bayesian Occupancy Grid. Thermal signal measurements \(z_t\) update survivor hypothesis probability \(P(\text{Survivor} \mid z_t)\) using Bayes' Rule:

\[ P(\text{Survivor} \mid z_t) = \frac{P(z_t \mid \text{Survivor}) P(\text{Survivor})}{P(z_t)} \]

This allows reliable survivor identification under severe visual obstruction.
